en: The Commentary on the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*, Scroll One;
also titled the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra-vyākhyāna*;
composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Seeing all sentient beings bound by afflictions, he gave rise to the vow for enlightenment to rescue and deliver them;
to such a Fully Awakened One, the Honored One of Compassion, I prostrate, for the purpose of composing this treatise to explain the sūtras.
My treatise can exhaust the enmity of the afflictions and rescue all beings from the evil paths;
such supreme benefits as these two do not exist within the treatises of any non-Buddhists.
This sūtra comprises nine sections:
first, the introductory section;
second, the section on the accomplishment of the disciples who are to hear it.
3. The section on samādhi;
4. The section on the purity of the contemplator;
5. The section on the phenomena to be contemplated.
Six, the Section on Origination;
Seven, the Section on Exposition;
Eight, the Section on the Power of the Bodhisattva’s Merit;
9. The Section on the Distinctions of Bodhisattva Practice.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was staying at Gayāśīrṣa on the summit of Mount Gayā, at the stūpa where he first attained awakening, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus. Previously, they had all been brahmins with matted hair; they had done what was to be done, accomplished their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge their minds were liberated. They had attained mastery over all their minds and had reached the further shore—all of them were arhats.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were immeasurable and boundless, having all come together from the worlds of the ten directions; they possessed great majestic power, had all attained the various patiences (kṣānti), the various dhāraṇīs, and the various profound samādhis, and were endowed with the various supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Their names were:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Gandhahastin Bodhisattva, Sūradatta Bodhisattva, Sūrapratipatti-jñāna Bodhisattva, and others who served as the leaders.
Thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were immeasurable in number,
surrounded by a great assembly including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
The Commentary states:
"Thus have I heard at one time," and so forth, are the words of the compiler of the Dharma.
The phrase "dwelling in the city of Gayā" demonstrates the perfection of the place of residence.
The summit of Mount Gayā is shown because it is the place where that assembly dwells and moves about;
the stūpa is shown because it serves as the object for those who offer worship to perform their offerings.
"One who has first attained bodhi" refers to the very moment of his attaining buddhahood.
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus" means that because it is a great assembly—
and because it neither increases nor decreases— it consists of a full thousand bhikṣus.
The "brahmin with braided hair" refers here to bhikṣus who are learners (śaikṣa) and those beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
This is called the perfection of the listener.
The remainder of the passage will next explain the distinctions among the various practices of bodhisattvas.
That bodhisattva practice is subsumed by two kinds of encompassing methods. What are these two?
First, the encompassment of causes; [and second, the encompassment of results].
Second is the inclusion of the fruit.

Furthermore, as for the stūpa on the summit of Mount Gayā, it constitutes the introductory section of the root text; because it is the dwelling place of immeasurable Buddhas, it manifests the assembly of those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, at that location.
This Dharma-gate is protected by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Those who should hear this sūtra will achieve its full realization; both those in training and those beyond training were formerly brahmins with matted hair.
Furthermore, those beyond training possess eight kinds of virtues. What are these eight?
First, their task is completed, as the Sūtra says: "That which was to be done has been done."
Second, they have ultimately transcended what ought to be done because they have already accomplished what was to be done, as the sūtra says, "what was to be done has been completed.
Third, they are far removed from the obstacles to samādhi because they have cast off the heavy burden, as the sūtra says, "the heavy burden has been laid down."
Fourth is the relinquishing of the heavy burden one has taken up, as the sutra says, "attaining one's own benefit.
That heavy burden refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Fifth is the realization of nirvana, as the sutra says, "exhausting all fetters of existence" (*bhava-saṃyojana*)."
Sixth, transcending the three realms, as the sutra states: "By means of right wisdom, the mind attains liberation.

Seventh, relying on non-perverted teachings to practice, as the sutra states: "All minds have attained mastery and reached the other shore," because they have skillfully distanced themselves from all afflictions.
Eighth, they practice the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) as they truly are, as the sutra states, "All are arhats.
Furthermore, because an arhat is one who is worthy of receiving the offerings bestowed by others, he is called "one to whom offerings should be made" (*arhat*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of training. What are the two?
First, the training of the path through the ultimate maintenance of ethical discipline.
Second, because whatever the mind seeks is ultimately fulfilled.
Next, the section on samādhi is explained.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the World-Honored One, alone and in solitude with no one present, entered the profound samādhi of all Buddhas and contemplated the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The commentary states:
"Entering samādhi to contemplate" demonstrates that this is not a realm accessible to discursive thought or intellectual deliberation.
Furthermore, "entering samādhi" is shown to demonstrate that [the Buddha] is not the same as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
this clarifies that it is not the realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The section on samādhi has been explained.
Next, the section on the purity of the contemplator is explained.
The Sūtra says:
And he forms this thought:

I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and acquired all-encompassing wisdom; my task is accomplished, the heavy burden is laid down, and I have crossed over the perilous paths of existence. I have extinguished ignorance and attained true illumination; I have extracted the arrows and severed craving. I have completed the Dharma-ship, struck the Dharma-drum, blown the Dharma-conch, and raised the Dharma-banner. I have transformed the seeds of birth-and-death and revealed the nature of *nirvāṇa*; I have blocked the evil paths and opened the right way; I have led away from the fields of sin and pointed toward the field of merit.
The Commentary states:
"One who can contemplate purity" demonstrates that he has already attained bodhi, as the Sūtra says:
"He then forms this thought: 'I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
One who attains bodhi does so to manifest a superior realization-wisdom compared to that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as the sūtra states: "attaining all-encompassing wisdom.
There are seventeen kinds of this attainment of all-encompassing wisdom.
What are the seventeen?
First, the fulfillment of original vows, as the sūtra says, "that which was to be done has been accomplished.
Second, the relinquishing of the heavy burden of grasping, as the sūtra says, "having laid down all heavy burdens."
Furthermore, the heavy burden refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Third, they skillfully sever all obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), as the sutra says: "They cross over the perilous paths of existence."
Fourth is the skillful severance of all obstructions to omniscience, as the sūtra says, "extinguishing ignorance.
Fifth is the realization of the sublime Dharma as it truly is, as the sūtra says, "attaining true illumination."
Sixth is being free from all perverse arrows, as the sūtra says, "extracting all arrows.
Seventh is being free from all delusions, as the sūtra says, "severing thirst and craving."
Eighth is the accomplishment of supramundane wisdom, as the sūtra says, "becoming a vessel of the Dharma.
Ninth is the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma, as the sūtra says, "beating the drum of the Dharma."
Tenth, he utters the wondrous sound of selflessness, skillfully subduing all māras, as indicated by the sūtra’s mention of “blowing the dharma conch.
Eleventh, he is well able to subdue all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), as indicated by the sūtra’s mention of “erecting the dharma banner.”
Twelfth is the skillful severance of all causes and conditions for the fetters (*saṃyojana*), as the sūtra says, "transforming the seeds of birth and death.
Thirteenth is the teaching of the sublime dharmas of the mundane and supramundane, as the sūtra says, "manifesting the nature of *nirvāṇa*."
Fourteenth, he is well able to remain far removed from inverted grasping at signs, as the sūtra says, "blocking off the evil paths.
Fifteenth, he turns toward the Eightfold Noble Path, as the sūtra says, "opening up the right path."
Sixteenth, he is well able to distance himself from the fields of merit of non-Buddhists, as the sutra says, "having departed from all fields of sin.
Seventeenth, he manifests the fields of merit of the Triple Gem, as the sutra says, "showing the field of merit."
The section on the purity of the contemplator has already been explained.
Next, the section on the phenomena to be contemplated is explained.
The Sūtra says:
I shall now contemplate that dharma:
who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? By what kind of wisdom does one attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
What is the dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* that is to be realized?
The treatise says:
By what kind of person can bodhi be realized?
By what kind of wisdom is bodhi realized?
What is that bodhi which is realized?
Contemplating those three dharmas, one sees that within the three periods of time they are falsely discriminated and lack any substantial reality.
The Sūtra says:
"Is it attained by means of the body, or is it attained by means of the mind?

If it were attained by means of the body, the body would be without cognition or awareness—like grass, like wood, like a clod of earth, or like a shadow—possessing no discernment. It is composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, and its nature is impermanent; it exists only through the provisional support of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and bathing."
This dharma will inevitably lead to ruin and extinction.
The Treatise states:
When the Sūtra asks, "Is it attained by means of the body, or is it attained by means of the mind? it demonstrates that neither body nor mind realizes Bodhi.
What does this clarify?
It means that apart from body and mind, there is nothing else that is real.
This is because, as falsely conceptualized by deluded people, there is no such thing as one who realizes enlightenment.
By what kind of person can awakening be realized?
Since those phenomena are falsely discriminated throughout the three periods of time and lack substantial reality, it is shown that awakening is attained not by means of a body.
There are eight kinds of dharmas that demonstrate that his body does not realize bodhi.
What are these eight?
First is the absence of an agent, as the sūtra says: "If it were realized by means of the body, the body would be without cognition and without awareness."
Second is the accomplishment of grasping at false signs, as the sūtra says, "like grass, like wood, like a clod of earth, like a shadow.
Third is the distancing from all conceptualizations, as the sūtra says, "there is no cognition or knowledge."
Fourth, it arises through the conjunction of various causes and conditions, as the Sūtra says, "produced by the four great elements.
Fifth, its substance is fundamentally impure, as the Sūtra says, "born from father and mother."
Sixth is that mindfulness does not abide, as the sūtra says, "Its nature is impermanent.
Seventh is that it is like a precarious and decaying object that cannot be maintained permanently, as the sūtra says, "It exists only by means of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and bathing."
Eighth, its essence is unreal, as the sūtra states: "These dharmas inevitably tend toward decay, ruin, and extinction.
Thus, it has been explained that awakening is attained not by means of a body, but is manifested [through such realization].
Regarding those individuals who attain enlightenment, those phenomena within the three periods of time are devoid of substantial reality due to false conceptualization.
Next, it explains by means of what kind of wisdom one realizes enlightenment.
Regarding those dharmas which, throughout the three periods of time, are falsely discriminated and lack substantial reality, they manifest the attainment of bodhi through that which is not the mind.
The Sūtra says:
"If one were to attain it by means of the mind, then the mind would be like an illusion, arising from a multitude of conditions; it has no location, no marks, no substance, and nothingness."
The treatise says:
There are six kinds of dharmas that demonstrate how that mind does not attain bodhi.
What are these six?
First, seeing that the dharmas of perversion are false and deceptive, deluding foolish ordinary beings, as the sutra says: "The mind is like an illusion.
Second, arising in dependence upon various causes and conditions, whether wholesome or unwholesome, as the sutra says: "Arising from manifold conditions."
Third, there is no fixed place of abiding, as the sutra says, "no location.
Fourth, false conceptualization grasps at signs that are ultimately unobtainable, as the sutra says, "signlessness."
Fifth is emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), as the sūtra says "no thing" (*nirvastuka*).
Sixth is the far-reaching (*dūraṅgama*), as the sūtra says "nothing exists" (*akiñcana*).
Thus has been explained the manifestation of attaining awakening through that which is not mind.
Regarding the wisdom by which one attains bodhi: those phenomena within the three periods of time are falsely discriminated and lack any substantial reality.
Next, it is explained what that realized bodhi is.
Those phenomena, throughout the three periods of time, are falsely discriminated and lack any substantial reality.
As the Sūtra says:
"Bodhi is merely a name; it is spoken of for the sake of worldly convention."

It is without sound, without form, without accomplishment, without activity, and without entry; it cannot be seen and cannot be relied upon. Its paths of coming and going are severed, transcending all verbal expression. It has emerged from the three realms; it is without seeing, without hearing, without cognition, without attachment, and without observation. It is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), without contention and without demonstration. It cannot be contemplated and cannot be seen; it is without resonance and without characters, transcending the path of language.
The Commentary states:

When the Sūtra says, "Bodhi is merely a name, spoken of for the sake of conventional truth," it demonstrates that the dharmas to be realized exist only as names; because they are produced by false conceptualization, their essence is not real.
That exists only as a name; it is spoken of for the sake of worldly convention.
There are twenty-three kinds. What are these twenty-three?
First is the absence of objective entities, as the sūtra says, "there is no sound.
Second is the transcendence of the sphere of perception, as the sūtra says, "there is no form.
Third is the emptiness of the essence of all phenomena, as the sūtra says, "there is no formation."
Fourth is being free from all signs (*nimitta*), as the sūtra says "without activity" (*apracāra*).
Fifth is transcending the sphere of all worldly ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), as the sūtra says "without entry" (*anupraveśa*).
Sixth, it transcends the sphere of consciousness, as the sūtra says, "it cannot be seen.
Seventh, it has no basis upon which to rely, as the sūtra says, "it cannot be relied upon."
Eighth is non-arising and non-ceasing, as the sūtra says, "the paths of coming and going are severed.
Ninth is transcending all worldly names, as the sūtra says, "transcending all verbal expressions."
Tenth, the non-apprehensibility of all phenomena, whether wholesome or unwholesome actions, as the Sūtra says, "having emerged from the three realms.
Eleventh, being free from the viewer, as the Sūtra says, "without seeing."
Twelfth, it transcends the sphere of auditory consciousness, as the sūtra says, "there is no hearing.
Thirteenth, it transcends the sphere of mental consciousness, as the sūtra says, "there is no cognition."
Fourteenth is non-abiding, as the sūtra says "without attachment.
Fifteenth is like space, as the sūtra says "without observation.
Sixteenth is unconditioned, as the sūtra says "free from conceptual proliferation."
Seventeenth, it is free from all afflictions and detached from all outflows, as the sūtra says "without contention.
Eighteenth, it transcends the sphere of limited wisdom, as the sūtra says "without demonstration."
Nineteenth is immeasurability, as the sutra says, "it cannot be observed.
Twentieth is that others cannot see it, as the sutra says, "it cannot be seen."
Twenty-first: the internal mind is without cognition, as the sūtra says, "there is no resonance.
Twenty-second: there is nothing that can be seen, as the sūtra says, "there are no characters."
The twenty-third is that which is ineffable, as the Sūtra states because it is "beyond language.
The Sūtra says:

"In this way, that which can realize bodhi, the wisdom by which one realizes bodhi, and the dharma of bodhi that is realized—all such dharmas exist only as names; they are spoken of only as provisional names, spoken of only as composite names, spoken of by relying on conventional names, and spoken of through the discrimination of non-discrimination. They are conventionally established yet not established; they are without substance and apart from substance; they are without grasping, ineffable, and without attachment."
In that state, there is no person who realizes, no means by which to realize, and no dharma that can be realized.

To penetrate this thoroughly is what is called attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is without differentiation or separation from differentiation, and it possesses no characteristic of enlightenment.
The Commentary says:

Next, as for how one realizes bodhi, that too exists only as a provisional designation and a name; it is spoken of according to worldly convention, for false discrimination has no substantial reality.
Based on conventional designations, there are six kinds. What are these six?
First is unreal conceptualization, as the Sūtra says: "It is called non-conceptual conceptualization."
Second is the emptiness of essence, as the sūtra says, "conditioned formation is non-formation.
Third is the unobtainability of a self, as the sūtra says, "neither entity nor devoid of entity."
Fourth is the transcendence of worldly wisdom, as the sūtra states "without grasping.
Fifth is the transcendence of the path of language, as the sūtra states "inexpressible."
Sixth is the distancing from self and what belongs to self, as the sūtra says, "without attachment.
Furthermore, the sūtra states: "In that place, there is no person who realizes, there is nothing used for realization, and there is no dharma to be realized."
"To thus penetrate [reality] is what is called attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies the person who realizes, the wisdom used for realization, and the objective realm that is realized.

Regarding those dharmas, by means of what dharma does one, through sublime and correct wisdom, know them as they truly are—what is seen, what is known, and what is realized? This is called attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, as for the statement in the Sūtra, "There is no difference, there is no separation from difference, and there is no characteristic of bodhi," what meaning does this clarify?
The two phrases, "no difference" and "no separation from difference," clarify that the dharma realized therein is pure and quiescent.
The meaning of the absence of the characteristics of enlightenment is as previously explained.
The section on the objects of observation has already been discussed.
Next, regarding the section on the arising [of the path], what further meaning does it contain?
Because the matter of samādhi has been concluded and because the time for teaching has arrived, he should therefore arise.
Furthermore, there are two meanings herein:
first, because he wishes to explain for Mañjuśrī the meaning observed within samādhi; [second, ...]
Second, because it consists of Mañjuśrī’s questions and the Tathāgata’s answers.
For what reason does the Tathāgata address only Mañjuśrī and not others?
It is because this Dharma was taught in reliance upon Mañjuśrī as his interlocutor.
Furthermore, for what reason was this Dharma-gate taught specifically to Mañjuśrī?
Because this Dharma-gate that is being taught is profound, it was therefore addressed to that Bodhisattva of deep wisdom.
Furthermore, for what reason does only Mañjuśrī inquire?
It is because the Tathāgata addressed only Mañjuśrī;
therefore, Mañjuśrī inquires in accordance with the meaning.
The question he raised was asked with a pure mind, because the answer was pure.
Next is the section on the explicit exposition.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī was in the great assembly, standing to the right of the Buddha and holding a great precious parasol to shade the Buddha.
Then, silently knowing the thoughts in the World-Honored One’s mind, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If awakening has such characteristics, how should sons and daughters of good family generate the mind of awakening and abide within it?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Sons and daughters of good family should know the characteristics of awakening in this way, and thus generate the mind of awakening and abide within it."
Mañjuśrī said: "World-Honored One!
How should one know the characteristics of bodhi?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"The characteristic of Bodhi transcends the triple world and surpasses all worldly names and language; it surpasses all sounds and is without the arousal of thought. To extinguish all such arisings is to dwell in the arousal of the bodhicitta."
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas transcend all such productions of the thought of awakening; this is the dwelling of the production of the thought of awakening. Mañjuśrī!
Non-arising is the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Mañjuśrī! For one who has aroused the bodhicitta, the dwelling of non-arising of any thing is the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Mañjuśrī! For one who has resolved upon bodhicitta, dwelling without obstruction is the dwelling of one who has resolved upon bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!
One who generates the bodhicitta abides in accordance with the nature of phenomena; this is the abiding of generating the bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!
One who generates the bodhicitta does not cling to any phenomena; this is the abiding of generating the bodhicitta.
Mañjuśrī! One who has resolved upon bodhicitta does not destroy the reality-limit; this is the dwelling of one who has resolved upon bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!
To generate the bodhicitta that is neither shifting nor increasing, neither different nor one—this is the dwelling of generating the bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!

One who generates the bodhicitta should dwell having generated the bodhicitta in this way: like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like a shadow, like an echo, like space, and like the moon in water.
The treatise says:
That arousal of purity is of nine kinds. What are the nine?
First, the relinquishing of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), as the sutra states: "Mañjuśrī!
Non-arising is the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Second, the relinquishing of grasping at phenomena, as the sutra states: "Mañjuśrī!"
"One who gives rise to the bodhicitta does so by dwelling in the non-dwelling of any thing; this is the dwelling of one who has given rise to the bodhicitta.
Third, it is like space, as the sutra says: "Mañjuśrī!"
"One who has resolved upon bodhicitta abides in non-obstruction; this is the abiding of one who has resolved upon bodhicitta.
Fourth is tranquility, as the sūtra says: "Mañjuśrī!"
"One who generates the bodhicitta abides in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); this is the 'abiding in the generation of the bodhicitta.
Fifth is the relinquishing and grasping of the marks of permanence and impermanence, as the sutra says: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"One who generates the bodhicitta does not cling to any phenomena; this is the dwelling of one who has generated the bodhicitta.
Sixth is not disparaging the path and not abandoning the path, as the sutra says: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"One who generates the bodhicitta does not destroy suchness, which is the limit of reality; this is the dwelling of generating the bodhicitta.
Seventh is freedom from slander and freedom from attachment, as the sutra says: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"One who generates the bodhicitta does not shift, does not increase, is neither different nor one; this is the dwelling of generating the bodhicitta.
Eighth is entering the single characteristic of all phenomena, as the sutra says: "Mañjuśrī!..."

"One who has generated the bodhicitta should dwell having generated the bodhicitta in this way: like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like a shadow, like an echo, like space, and like the moon in water," and thus one should also practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) according to reality.
Regarding the remaining four lines concerning "transcending the three realms" and so forth, they should be understood as previously explained.
The section on the explicit exposition is concluded.
Next, the section on the power of the bodhisattva’s qualities is presented.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Candraprabhāśrīguṇa, who had attained non-retrogression from the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. He asked Mañjuśrī, saying:
"For what reason do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first contemplate which dharma before practicing the bodhisattva conduct?"
"By relying on what dharma does one practice the bodhisattva conduct? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
The practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has great compassion as its foundation for the sake of all sentient beings.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the basis of the great compassion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"The great compassion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has a straightforward mind as its foundation.
The celestial son asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the basis of the straightforward mind of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
The straightforward mind of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has the mind of equality toward all sentient beings as its foundation.
The celestial son asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the basis for the impartial mind that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas maintain toward all sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, which is based on non-differentiation and the practice of being free from differentiation.
The celestial son asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the basis for the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which is non-dual and free from duality? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice without distinction and free from differentiation, taking the profound and pure mind as their foundation.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the root of the profound and pure mind of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
The profound and pure minds of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as their foundation.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
“What serves as the foundation for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening mind of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!”
"The minds of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas directed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi have the six pāramitās as their foundation.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What do the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take as their foundation? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Devaputra!"
“The six pāramitās of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have skillful means and wisdom as their foundation.
The devaputra asked again: “Mañjuśrī!”
"What is the basis for the skillful means and wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"The skillful means and wisdom of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have non-negligence as their foundation.
The celestial son asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the foundation for the non-negligence of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice heedfulness, taking the three types of wholesome conduct as their foundation.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the basis for the three types of wholesome conduct of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"The three types of wholesome conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have the ten paths of wholesome action as their foundation.
The celestial son asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What serves as the foundation for the ten paths of wholesome action of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"The ten paths of wholesome action for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have the observance of precepts as their foundation.
The celestial son asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the foundation for the precept-keeping of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"The precept-keeping of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has right mindfulness as its foundation.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the basis for the right mindfulness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"For all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, right mindfulness has right observation as its foundation.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
“What is the foundation of the correct contemplation of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!”
The correct contemplation of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has firm mindfulness and non-forgetfulness as its foundation.
The treatise states:
The power of the merits of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is of two kinds.
What are these two?
First, the fulfillment of all that is sought according to one's heart's desire;
second, the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech for preaching the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "all that the mind seeks is fully satisfied," this is because one gives rise to ever-increasing, most excellent dharmas.
There are fourteen types of such ever-increasing, most excellent dharmas that are brought forth.
What are the fourteen?
First is not forgetting what has been received through instruction, as the sutra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the basis for the correct contemplation of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Devaputra!"
"Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas correctly contemplate, taking firm mindfulness and non-forgetfulness as their foundation.
Second, they skillfully grasp the correct teaching and contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), as the sūtra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the basis for the right mindfulness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas maintain right mindfulness, taking right contemplation as their foundation.
Third, there is no fault regarding that state, as the sūtra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the foundation for the precept-keeping of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas maintain the precepts, taking right mindfulness as their foundation.
Fourth, not following after various faults, as the sutra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
“What do the ten paths of wholesome action of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take as their basis? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!”
"Because the ten paths of wholesome action for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have the observance of precepts as their foundation.
Fifth is the skillful cultivation of the ten paths of wholesome action, as the sutra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the foundation of the three types of wholesome conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"Because the three types of wholesome conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have the ten paths of wholesome action as their foundation.
Sixth is the purity of the three dharmas of body, speech, and mind, as the sutra states: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the foundation for the non-negligence of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are heedful, taking the three types of wholesome conduct as their foundation.
Seventh is the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), as the sutra states: "The devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the foundation of the skillful means and wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Devaputra!"
"Because the skillful means and wisdom of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have non-negligence as their foundation.
Eighth is to accord with and benefit all sentient beings, as the sutra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What serves as the foundation for the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"Because the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have skillful means and wisdom as their foundation.
Ninth, fulfilling all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), as the sūtra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the root of the mind of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"Because the mind of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has the six pāramitās as its foundation.
Tenth is non-exhaustion, as the sūtra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the foundation of the profound and pure mind of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Devaputra!"
"Because the profound and pure mind of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas takes the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as its foundation.
Eleventh is the purity of karmic fruit, as the sutra states: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
“What is the basis for the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which is without distinction and free from distinction? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!”
"Because all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice without distinction or departure from non-distinction, taking the profoundly pure mind as their foundation.
Twelfth is the purity of cultivation, as the sutra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the basis for the impartial mind that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas maintain toward all sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"Because all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas take as their foundation an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, free from differentiation and devoid of dualistic conduct.
Thirteenth is the purification that benefits all sentient beings, as the sutra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the foundation of the straightforward mind of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"The upright mind of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has the mind of equality toward all sentient beings as its basis.
Fourteenth is the purity of mind, as the sutra states: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"What is the basis of the great compassion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Devaputra!"
"The great compassion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has a straightforward mind as its foundation.

Furthermore, a sūtra states: "At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Candraprabhaśrī (Moon Pure Radiance Virtue), who had attained non-retrogression in his resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He asked Mañjuśrī:
'By taking what dharma as their primary object do all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path?'"
"By relying on what dharma does one practice the bodhisattva conduct? Mañjuśrī replied:

"The practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has great compassion as its foundation, for the sake of all sentient beings. One should understand that such sūtras are to be explained by proceeding from the end toward the beginning.
Having already explained how all that is sought by the mind is fully satisfied,
next is explained the unobstructed eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*) for teaching the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:
The Devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, how many kinds of minds do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess that can accomplish the cause and can accomplish the fruit?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "O Devaputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess four kinds of mind that can accomplish the cause and can accomplish the fruit."
What are the four?
First, the initial arousal of the mind;
second, the arousal of the mind through practice.
Third is the resolve of non-retrogression;
fourth is the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The initial arousal of the mind is like various seeds; the second, the arousal of the mind through practice, is like the sprouting and growth of a shoot; the third, the arousal of the mind of non-retrogression, is like the initial accomplishment of stems, leaves, flowers, and fruit; and the fourth, the arousal of the mind of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the utility of such fruits.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The initial aspiration is like the carpenter’s wisdom in gathering materials; the second, the aspiration of practice, is like the wisdom in cutting and refining the timber; the third, the aspiration of non-retrogression, is like the wisdom in arranging and installing the materials; and the fourth, the aspiration of the stage of one birth remaining before Buddhahood, is like the wisdom in completing the carriage for transport.

Furthermore, O Son of Heaven! The initial resolve is like the newly risen moon; the second, the resolve of practice, is like the moon on the fifth day; the third, the resolve of non-retrogression, is like the moon on the tenth day; the fourth, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the moon on the fourteenth day; and the wisdom of the Tathāgata is like the moon on the fifteenth day.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The first resolve, the initial aspiration, can transcend the stage of the śrāvaka; the second resolve, the resolve of practice, can transcend the stage of the pratyekabuddha; the third resolve, the non-retrogressive resolve, can transcend the indeterminate stage; and the fourth resolve, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, abides securely in the determinate stage.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The first production of the thought of enlightenment is like the knowledge of learning the initial chapters; the second, the production of the thought of practice, is like the knowledge of distinguishing the various chapters; the third, the production of the thought of non-retrogression, is like the knowledge of calculation; and the fourth, the production of the thought of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the knowledge of penetrating all treatises.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The first arousal of the mind arises from causes; the second, the arousal of the mind through practice, arises from wisdom; the third, the arousal of the mind of non-retrogression, arises from abandonment; and the fourth, the arousal of the mind of the stage of one birth before Buddhahood, arises from the fruit.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The first arousal of the mind is subsumed under causes; the second, the arousal of the mind through practice, is subsumed under wisdom; the third, the irreversible arousal of the mind, is subsumed under abandonment; and the fourth, the arousal of the mind at the stage of one birth remaining before Buddhahood, is subsumed under fruition.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the cause arises; from the second, the practice, the wisdom of the thought of enlightenment arises; from the third, the non-retrogressive, the severance of arising arises; and from the fourth, the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, the fruit of the thought of enlightenment arises.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

First is the section on the distinctions of the causal stage of the initial arousal of the mind; second is the section on the distinctions of the wisdom of the arousal of the mind during the stage of practice; third is the section on the distinctions of the severance of obstacles in the irreversible arousal of the mind; and fourth is the section on the distinctions of the fruit of the arousal of the mind at the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The initial aspiration is like the expedient means of gathering medicinal herbs; the second, the aspiration of practice, is like the expedient means of distinguishing the medicinal herbs; the third, the non-retrogressive aspiration, is like the expedient means of taking medicine when ill; and the fourth, the aspiration of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the expedient means of recovering from the illness.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The first resolve is the resolve of initial aspiration, wherein one trains as one born into the family of a Dharma King. The second is the resolve of practice, wherein one trains in the Dharma of the Dharma King. The third is the resolve of non-retrogression, wherein one is able to fully master the training in the Dharma of the Dharma King. The fourth is the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, wherein one trains in the Dharma of the Dharma King and attains sovereign mastery.
The treatise says:

There are four ways of generating the bodhicitta through the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*) when teaching the Dharma, which encompass the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because they are explained through various distinctions.
Those various distinctions consist of twelve phrases.
The Sūtra says: "The Devaputra asked again: 'Mañjuśrī!'"
"How many kinds of minds do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess that can accomplish the cause and can accomplish the fruit?
Mañjuśrī replied: "O Devaputra!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess four kinds of mind that can accomplish the cause and can accomplish the fruit.
What are the four? The first is the initial generation of the mind.
"Second, the mind of practice;
third, the non-retrogressive mind;

and fourth, the mind of the stage of one-life-to-enlightenment. Herein, the initial generation of the mind serves as the cause for the second, the mind of practice; the mind of practice serves as the cause for the third, the non-retrogressive mind; and the non-retrogressive mind serves as the cause for the fourth, the mind of the stage of one-life-to-enlightenment.
This passage clarifies that because the progressively superior causes do not fail, they lead to progressively superior results.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Moreover, O Son of Heaven! The initial resolve is like various seeds;

the second, the resolve of practice, is like the sprouting and growth of a shoot; the third, the non-retrogressive resolve, is like the initial perfection of the stem, leaves, flowers, and fruit; the fourth, the resolve of the stage of one birth remaining [before Buddhahood], is like the fruit and so forth being of practical use. This demonstrates that from pure causes, pure fruits are accomplished.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "Moreover, O Son of Heaven!
The initial generation of the mind of awakening is like a carpenter gathering materials for wisdom," because by relying on various vows, one is able to gather all the Buddha-dharmas.
"The second generation of the mind of enlightenment is like the wisdom that fashions and refines timber," because it achieves pure ethical discipline.

"The third non-retrogressive generation of the mind of enlightenment is like the wisdom that securely places the timber," because all practices cultivated through reliance on wisdom and skillful means are in perfect accord.

Regarding the statement, "The fourth, the resolve of one in their final birth before Buddhahood, is like a chariot that accomplishes transport because it does not abandon the heavy burden previously undertaken," the Sūtra further says: "Furthermore, O Devaputra!"

"The initial resolve is like the new moon; the second, the resolve of practice, is like the moon on the fifth day; the third, the resolve of non-retrogression, is like the moon on the tenth day; the fourth, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the moon on the fourteenth day; and the wisdom of the Tathāgata is like the moon on the fifteenth day. This is said to demonstrate the manifestation of progressively superior, great power, and purity.
Furthermore, when a sutra states, "Moreover, O Devaputra,

the initial generation of the mind can transcend the stage of the śrāvaka," this is because the bodhisattva prior to the first stage possesses sharp faculties and observes all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).

Regarding the statement, "The second practice of generating the mind can transcend the stage of the pratyekabuddha," this is because a bodhisattva prior to the first stage, by relying on the superior wisdom of *prajñā*, is able to accumulate the immeasurable practices of all bodhisattvas.

Regarding the statement, “The third non-retrogressive generation of the mind can transcend the stage of indeterminate attainment,” this is because one has already entered the first stage (*bhūmi*) and attained realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase “transcending the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,” this is because one has transcended all practices involving effortful application (*prayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "the fourth [stage], the stage of one destined for rebirth in the next life, wherein the mind is resolved and abides in the stage of meditative concentration," this refers to the stage of Prince Sudhana.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Moreover, O Son of Heaven!"
"The first arousal of the mind is like the knowledge of the first dhyāna" means that it involves contemplating the dharmas of the lower stages.
"The second practice of arousing the mind is like the knowledge of the various chapters" means that it involves the differentiation through the increase of wisdom.
"The third, the resolve of non-retrogression, is like the wisdom of calculation" means that through the wisdom of skillful means, one is able to calculate all phenomena.
"The fourth, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more [ekajātipratibaddha], is like the wisdom of penetrating all treatises" means that one has attained the wisdom of realization.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Moreover, O Son of Heaven!
The first arousal of the mind arises from causes," because it is inherently pure and accomplished from the very beginning.
"The second, the arousal of the mind through practice, arises from wisdom," because it encompasses the skillful means of mundane and supramundane wisdom derived from hearing.
"The third, the non-retrogressive resolve for awakening, arises from the cessation [of afflictions]," because it transcends all worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

"The fourth, the resolve for awakening of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), arises from the fruit," because one spontaneously accomplishes all practices.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Moreover, O Son of Heaven!

'The cause of the initial generation of the mind is subsumed' means that it is because the path of practice through faith has reached maturity, and also because one contemplates the realm of the first stage (bhūmi)."

Regarding "the second stage, the resolve for awakening is subsumed by the mind": this is because one practices the application of effort through the matured contemplation based on the objective realm.

Regarding "the third stage, the resolve for awakening is subsumed by abandonment": this is because one contemplates that the Buddha-dharma has not yet been attained despite relying on the practice of the objective realm.

Regarding "the fourth, the result comprised within the resolve of the stage of being born only once more (ekajātipratibaddha)": because the fruit of maturation is perfected, one attains Buddhahood immediately in whichever Buddha-field is appropriate for becoming a Buddha.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"Moreover, O Devaputra, the cause for the initial arousal of the mind arises" because of the nature of the roots of goodness cultivated through non-perverted practice.
"The wisdom of the second arousal of the mind for practice arises" because of the ultimate nature of non-perverted dharmas.
"The third, the arising of the non-regressive resolve that severs birth," is so called because its nature consists of non-perverted practice.
"The fourth, the arising of the fruit of the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood," is so called because one has attained mastery over the mind.

Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Moreover, O Devaputra, regarding the 'Section on the Differentiation of Causes for the Initial Resolve': it is because of the gathering of immeasurable roots of goodness.
Regarding the 'Section on the Differentiation of Wisdom for the Second Stage of Practice': it is because of the ultimate perfection of immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates."
Regarding "The Third Section on the Distinctions of the Non-retrogressive Resolve," it is because one enters immeasurable gates of samādhi.

Regarding "The Fourth Section on the Distinctions of the Result of the Resolve of the Stage of One Birth Remaining," it is because one exercises mastery over the spontaneous display of immeasurable supernormal powers according to one's will.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Moreover, O Son of Heaven!

The initial generation of the mind of awakening is like the skillful means of gathering medicinal herbs," because it involves gathering the dharmas that serve as remedies for the disease of afflictions.

"The second stage of generating the aspiration for enlightenment is like the skillful means of distinguishing medicinal herbs" because it involves knowing the appropriate remedies that correspond to the diseases of the afflictions.

"The third stage of non-retrogressive generation of the aspiration is like the skillful means of taking medicine when ill" because it relies on knowing how to appropriately employ various skillful means according to what is required.

Regarding the phrase "The fourth [type of] bodhicitta, that of one in their final birth, is like the skillful means of recovering from an illness," it is because the disease of the afflictions has been extinguished.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Moreover, O Son of Heaven!..."
"First, generating the mind to study as one born into the family of the Dharma King" means that one thereby subdues all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Second, generating the mind to practice and study the Dharma of the Dharma King" means that one thereby studies everything to attain the state of supremacy.
"The third, the non-retrogressive resolve to attain enlightenment, is able to fully master the Dharma of the Dharma-King" because it attains the supreme fruit of the path of cultivation.

"The fourth, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is able to attain mastery in mastering the Dharma of the Dharma-King" because one attains unimpeded mastery over all phenomena.
The Treatise on the Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhi-sūtra, Volume One;
The Treatise on the Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhi-sūtra, Volume Two,
also known as the Treatise on the Gayā-śīrṣa-sūtra.
The Treatise composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty states:
The section on the power and influence of the bodhisattva’s merits has already been explained.
Next is the section on the distinctions in the practices of bodhisattvas.
The sutra says:
At that time, within the great assembly there was a devaputra named Lord of Samādhi-Light, who had not regressed from his resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Then the Devaputra King of the Light of Fixed Samādhi asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:
"What is the ultimate summary of the path for all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
"By means of this concise path, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
In brief, there are two paths for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
By means of these two paths, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these two?
First is the path of skillful means;
second is the path of wisdom.
Skillful means is knowing how to gather wholesome dharmas;
wisdom is the knowledge that knows all dharmas as they truly are.
Furthermore, skillful means is observing all sentient beings.
Wisdom is the knowledge that transcends all phenomena.
Furthermore, skillful means is the knowledge of the correspondence among all phenomena;
wisdom is the knowledge of the non-correspondence among all phenomena.
Furthermore, "skillful means" refers to the wisdom that contemplates the path of causes;
"wisdom" refers to the knowledge that extinguishes the path of causes.
The treatise says:
Since the World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, is personally present among the assembly, for what reason does he inquire of Mañjuśrī?
It is in order to manifest the merits of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
For what reason?
It is because it causes sentient beings who have conceived thoughts of contempt toward Bodhisattvas to give rise to a mind of respect and reverence.
There are two kinds of paths for the various distinctions in the practices of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are these two? First, the path of purity of causes;
second, the path of purity of qualities.
Regarding the path of purity of causes, it is so called because it demonstrates the purity of the supreme cause.
That purity of the supreme cause is explained by means of four types of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). What are these four?
First, the teaching on the path that aids purification;
second, the teaching on the path of meritorious wisdom;
third, the teaching on the path of realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Fourth is the teaching on the path of practice according to reality.
There are eight kinds of paths of pure merit. What are these eight?
First, it is the wisdom that gathers in and transforms all sentient beings, as the sutra says: "Furthermore, skillful means is the wisdom that knows how to gather wholesome dharmas.
Second, it is the ability to endure all unwholesome actions of sentient beings, as the sutra says: "Wisdom is the wisdom that knows all dharmas as they truly are."
Third is the gathering of all pure and white dharmas, as the sutra states: "Furthermore, skillful means is the wisdom that contemplates all sentient beings.
Fourth is the contemplation of all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), as the sutra states: "Wisdom is the knowledge that is detached from all dharmas."
Fifth is knowing the characteristic of the conjunction of all dharmas, as the sutra states: "Furthermore, skillful means is the knowledge that corresponds to all dharmas.
Sixth is knowing the characteristic of the non-conjunction of all dharmas, as the sutra states: "Wisdom is the knowledge that does not correspond to all dharmas."
Furthermore, the wise know that all phenomena are non-associated, while the sages do so because of their various vows.
Seventh, they know, as it truly is, those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed, as the Sūtra says: "Moreover, skillful means consists in the wisdom that observes the path of causes."
Eighth is the accumulation of various aids to the path (*bodhipakṣa*), as stated in the Sūtra: "Wisdom is the knowledge of the path that extinguishes the causes.
Thus, the path of the purity of merit has been explained.
Next, the path of the purity of the cause is explained.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, skillful means is the knowledge of the distinctions among all phenomena;
wisdom is the knowledge that all phenomena are without distinction.
Furthermore, skillful means refers to the adornment of Buddha-fields;
wisdom refers to the knowledge of the equality and non-differentiation of those Buddha-field adornments.
Furthermore, skillful means refers to entering into the faculties and activities of sentient beings.
As for wisdom, it does not perceive the cognition of sentient beings.
Furthermore, as for skillful means, one attains the site of enlightenment;
as for wisdom, one is able to realize the gnosis of all the Buddha-bodhi dharmas.
The treatise says:
The path of purification also has eight kinds. What are these eight?
First is the contemplation of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, as the sutra states: "Furthermore, skillful means is the wisdom that knows the distinctions among all dharmas.
Second is the departure from the root of all dharmas, which consists of causes and conditions, as the sutra states: "Wisdom is the wisdom that knows the non-distinction among all dharmas."
Third is being free from all obstacles, as the sutra states: "Furthermore, skillful means is the wisdom that adorns the Buddha-fields.
Fourth is severing all conjunctions, as the sutra states: "Wisdom is the wisdom of equality and non-differentiation that adorns the Buddha-fields."
Fifth is knowing things as they truly are, as the sūtra says: "Furthermore, skillful means is the wisdom that enters into the activities of the faculties of sentient beings.
Sixth is entering a single dharma-gate, as the sūtra says: "Wisdom is the knowledge that does not perceive sentient beings."

Seventh is knowing, as it truly is, the false conceptualizations of all ordinary beings, as the sutra states: "Furthermore, skillful means is the attainment of the wisdom of the site of enlightenment."
Eighth is the realization of the realm of tranquility, as the Sūtra says: "The wise are able to realize the wisdom of all the Buddha-dharmas of bodhi.
The Sūtra states:
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
It is said that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further have two kinds of concise paths.
By means of these two paths, all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are the two? First, the path of assistance;
second, the path of abandonment.
The path of assistance consists of the five pāramitās;
the path of abandonment consists of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abbreviated paths.
What are these two? First, the path with obstruction;
second, the unobstructed path.
The path with obstruction refers to the five pāramitās.
The path of non-obstruction is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abbreviated paths. What are these two?
The first is the path with outflows;
the second is the path without outflows.
The path with outflows consists of the five pāramitās.
The untainted path is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abbreviated paths. What are these two?
First is the path with measure;
second is the path without measure.
The path with measure involves grasping at signs and making conceptual distinctions.
The immeasurable path does not involve grasping at signs or conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of concise paths. What are these two?
The first is the path of wisdom;
the second is the path of abandonment.
The path of wisdom refers to that from the first stage through the seventh stage.
The path of abandonment refers to that from the eighth stage up to the tenth stage.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abbreviated paths; what are these two?
The first is the path of merit;
the second is the path of wisdom.
Regarding the path of merit, it consists of the accumulation of various roots of goodness, as the sutra states: "The aids to the path are the five pāramitās."
The path of wisdom is that which penetrates all phenomena, as the Sūtra states: "The path of abandonment is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "There are again two kinds of abbreviated paths."
"What are these two?
First is the path with obstruction;
second is the path without obstruction."
The five pāramitās that constitute the path with obstacles exist because they still involve activity within the three realms; these pertain to the stages prior to the first bhūmi.
The prajñāpāramitā that constitutes the path without obstacles exists because it transcends the three realms and enters the first bhūmi to realize gnosis.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "There are again two kinds of concise paths. What are the two?
First, the path with outflows (sāsrava-mārga); [the second is the path without outflows (anāsrava-mārga)]."
"Second is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
As for the tainted paths, which are the five *pāramitās*, because they accomplish worldly fruits, these pertain to the stages prior to the first ground."
The untainted path, which is the *prajñāpāramitā*, is so called because it accomplishes supramundane fruits and because one has thereby attained supramundane wisdom.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "There are again two kinds of abbreviated paths."
"What are these two?
First, the path with measure;
second, the immeasurable path."
The path with measure consists of conceptualizing by grasping at signs, because it universally grasps the objects of consciousness.
The path without measure consists of not conceptualizing by grasping at signs, because it transcends the objects of consciousness and does not perceive universal grasping.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "There are again two kinds of concise paths. What are the two?
First is the path of wisdom;..."
"Second is the path of abandonment.
The path of knowledge refers to those from the first stage through the seventh stage, because they know the conditioned realm as it truly is.
The path of abandonment refers to those from the eighth stage through the tenth stage, because they know the unconditioned realm as it truly is.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Vīryacaryājñāna, who addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"What is meant by the term 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva'?"
"What is meant by the wisdom of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? Mañjuśrī replied: "Good son!"
"Meaning" (artha) is called "non-correspondence," while "wisdom" (jñāna) is called "correspondence.
The Bodhisattva Vīryaprayuktajñāna said: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is meant by the non-correspondence of meaning and name?
What is meant by the correspondence of wisdom and name? Mañjuśrī replied:
Good son, "meaning" (artha) is called the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). That meaning does not correspond with any dharma, nor does it not correspond with any dharma. Why is this?
Because it is without change and without characteristics.
As for its meaning: there is not a single dharma with which it is associated, nor is there a single dharma with which it is not associated, because its meaning is fundamentally unestablished.

Therefore, there is not a single dharma that is associated with others, nor is there any meaning of a dharma that is not associated; it neither shifts nor increases, because there is not a single dharma that is associated, nor any that is not associated.
The Commentary states:
When the Sūtra says, "Good son!
Meaning (artha) is called 'non-correspondence,' while knowledge (jñāna) is called 'correspondence,'" it demonstrates that there are four aspects of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Furthermore, a sutra states: "Good son!
'Meaning' (artha) is a name for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). That meaning does not correspond with a single dharma, nor does it not correspond with a single dharma."

"Why is this? Because it is without change and without marks. This is because it is free from all faults of impermanence; therefore, the Sūtra says: "As for its meaning, there is not a single dharma with which it is associated, nor is there a single dharma with which it is not associated."
Because it abides by its own intrinsic nature, as the Sūtra says: "In the sense that it was originally unestablished.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "There is not a single dharma with which it is associated, nor is there a single dharma with which it is not associated."

Because it abides as the substantial reality of the eternally true *dharmadhātu*, the Sūtra states: "The meaning is neither diminished nor increased, for there is not a single dharma with which it is associated, nor is there a single dharma with which it is not associated."
Furthermore, there is not a single dharma that does not shift or increase, because the *dharmadhātu* neither increases nor decreases.
As the Sūtra says:
"O son of good family!"
Wisdom is called the Path.
The Path is that which is in mutual correspondence with the mind, not non-correspondence. Good son!
For this reason, wisdom is called "associated," not "unassociated.
Furthermore, son of good family,
wisdom is called "associated with cessation."
Therefore, noble son, wisdom is called a dharma that is associated, not a dharma that is dissociated.
Furthermore, noble son:

Wisdom is defined as the skillful contemplation of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, and what is possible and what is impossible.
Good son! For this reason, wisdom is called "concordant," not "inconcordant."
The Treatise says:
The Sūtra states, "Good son!
Wisdom is called the Path."

Regarding the statement, "The Way is that which is in mutual correspondence with the mind, not non-correspondence," from this point onward, it next explains the realization of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which consists of three types of phrases and six types of tenfold dharmas.
What is the meaning clarified here?
By what kind of wisdom, in what manner, for what purpose, and by abiding where can one realize the *dharmadhātu*?
Regarding "by what kind of wisdom," it is demonstrated through three types of phrases and six sets of ten dharmas.
What are the three kinds of phrases?
What kind of wisdom do they manifest?
Wisdom refers to the Path; the Path consists of mental factors that are associated with the mind, not dissociated from it. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Good son!..."
For this reason, wisdom is called "associated" and not "unassociated.
Furthermore, wisdom, together with its retinue, is able to realize the dharma-realm. Why is this so?
Because the mind is pure, the path is pure; because the path is pure, the mind is pure.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Moreover, noble son, wisdom is defined as being associated with abandonment."
"Therefore, son of good family!
Wisdom is called a dharma that is associated, not a dharma that is dissociated," because they mutually rely upon one another.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Moreover, son of good family!"
"Wisdom is defined as skillfully contemplating the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, and what is possible and what is impossible.
Good son! Therefore, wisdom is called 'concordant' and not 'discordant,' because it knows the objects of knowledge in accordance with reality."
The three kinds of phrases have already been explained.
Next, the six kinds of tenfold dharmas will be explained, beginning with the ten kinds of knowledge.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, good son,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of knowledge.
What are these ten?
First, the wisdom of causes;
second, the wisdom of results;
third, the wisdom of meanings.
Fourth is the wisdom of skillful means;
fifth is the wisdom of insight;
sixth is the wisdom of integration.
Seventh is the wisdom of the pāramitās;
eighth is the wisdom of great compassion;
ninth is the wisdom of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Tenth is the wisdom that does not cling to any phenomena.
Son of good family!
These are called the ten kinds of wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Treatise says:
The Sūtra states, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of knowledge.
What are these ten?"
1. "Wisdom of the Cause" refers to the excellent knowledge of the seeds of liberation that have existed since beginningless time.
2. "Wisdom of the Fruit" refers to knowing, as it truly is, the various karmic retributions that have occurred since beginningless time.
"Third, the wisdom of meaning (arthajñāna)" refers to being well-versed in benefiting oneself and others.
"Fourth, the wisdom of skillful means (upāyajñāna)" refers to being able to increase even minute roots of goodness until they become immeasurable.
"5. Wisdom of Insight (prajñājñāna)" refers to the ability to discern wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
"6. Wisdom of Comprehension (saṃgrahajñāna)" refers to the inclusion of both the gift of Dharma and the gift of material requisites.
"Seventh, the wisdom of the perfections (pāramitā)" refers to the skillful knowledge that brings various roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) to fulfillment.
"Eighth, the wisdom of great compassion (mahākaruṇā)" refers to the ability to give rise to virtuous conduct by relying upon those roots of goodness.
"9. Wisdom in transforming sentient beings" means skillfully observing the appropriate and inappropriate times.
"10. Wisdom that does not cling to any phenomena" means practicing the Middle Way by remaining free from the two extremes.
As the sutra states: "Good son!
These are called the ten kinds of knowledge of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Thus, the first ten kinds of knowledge have been explained.
Next, the twentieth kind of arousal [of the mind] is explained.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, son of good family!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of arousal [of resolve]. What are the ten?
First is the arousal of the body, because they desire to bring about the purification of the physical karma of all sentient beings.
The second is the arousal [of the mind] through speech, because one desires to cause the verbal karma of all sentient beings to be pure.
The third is the arousal [of the mind] through thought, because one desires to cause the mental karma of all sentient beings to be pure.
Fourth is internal manifestation, because of not falsely discriminating among any sentient beings.
Fifth is external manifestation, because of practicing equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Sixth is the arousal of wisdom, because of the fulfillment and purification of the Buddha-wisdom.
Seventh is the arousal of the pure land, because of manifesting the meritorious adornments of all the Buddha-lands.
Eighth is the resolve to transform sentient beings, because it knows the medicines for all the diseases of affliction.
Ninth is the true resolve, because it brings the assembly of certainty (*niyata-rāśi*) to fulfillment.
Tenth is the arousal of the mind through the fulfillment of unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*), because of non-attachment to all three realms (*tridhātu*). Noble son!
These are called the ten kinds of arousals of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
The treatise says:
The sūtra states, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of arousal [of the mind].
What are these ten?"
First is the arousal of the body, because one desires to cause the bodily karma of all sentient beings to be pure.
Second is the arousal of the mouth, because one desires to cause the verbal karma of all sentient beings to be pure.

"Third, the arousal of the mind, because one desires to cause the mental karma of all sentient beings to be pure" means that, in order to distance oneself from all evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, one arouses great diligence.

"Fourth, internal manifestation, which is for the purpose of transforming all sentient beings and causing them to train in that state. Regarding "not falsely discriminating among all sentient beings," it is because one does not cling to any phenomena.
"Fifth, external manifestation, because one practices with equanimity toward all sentient beings" means that one is free from hatred and attachment.
"Sixth, the manifestation of wisdom, because one is fully endowed with the purity of Buddha-wisdom" means that one teaches and transforms all sentient beings with equanimity.

"Seventh, the arousal of the aspiration for a pure land, in order to demonstrate the meritorious adornments of all Buddha-lands," means that one seeks the Dharma through the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) without inversion.
"第八，the arousal of the mind to transform and guide sentient beings, because of knowing the medicines for all afflictions," means that one has attained mastery over all dharmas.
"Ninth, the arousal of the mind through reality" means that one preaches the Dharma in accordance with the mind by knowing it as it truly is.

"Tenth, the arousal of the mind through the fulfillment of unconditioned wisdom" means that because one has aroused the true Dharma, one does not cling to any of the three realms; this is because the mind does not cling to false and illusory phenomena.
Furthermore, because the mind—whether real or unreal—is free from false grasping at signs, as the sutra says: "Good son!
These are called the ten kinds of arousal of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
The twentieth kind of production has already been explained.
Next, the thirtieth kind of practice will be explained.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, good son,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of practices. What are these ten?
First, the practice of the perfections;
second, the practice of the means of attraction;
third, the practice of wisdom.
Fourth, the practice of skillful means;
fifth, the practice of great compassion;
sixth, the practice of seeking the dharmas that aid wisdom.
Seventh is the practice of seeking the aid of wisdom;
eighth is the practice of mental purity;
ninth is the practice of contemplating the truths.
Tenth is the practice of non-attachment toward all things, whether pleasant or unpleasant.
Son of good family!
These are called the ten practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The treatise says:
The Sūtra states, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of practice. What are these ten?"
1. "The practice of the perfections" (pāramitācaryā) is so called because it fulfills the factors that assist awakening (bodhipakṣadharma).
2. "The practice of the means of integration" (saṃgrahavastucaryā) is so called because it is capable of teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
"Third, the practice of wisdom" means observing the phenomena of arising and ceasing as they truly are.
"Fourth, the practice of skillful means" means knowing all phenomena as they truly are.
"5. The Practice of Great Compassion" is so called because the mind does not seek to realize nirvāṇa for itself.
"6. The Practice of Seeking the Dharma of Supporting Wisdom" is so called because it is for the sake of attaining the four fearlessnesses.
"Seventh, the practice of seeking the aid of wisdom" means that one considers all dharmas to be spontaneously attained.
"Eighth, the practice of mental purity" means that one is free from doubt and confusion regarding all dharmas.
"9. The practice of contemplating all truths" refers to entering the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"10. The practice of non-attachment toward all things, whether pleasant or unpleasant" refers to being free from aversion and attachment, as previously explained.
As the sutra says: "Good son!
These are called the ten kinds of practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Thus, what kind of wisdom has been explained?
Next, it is explained how this is realized, through the manifestation of the forty-first kind of inexhaustible contemplation.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, son of good family!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have eleven kinds of inexhaustible contemplations.
What are these eleven? The first is the contemplation of the inexhaustibility of the body;
Second is the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of phenomena;
third is the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of afflictions;
fourth is the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of the Dharma.
Fifth is the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of affection;
sixth is the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of vision;
seventh is the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Eighth is the contemplation of inexhaustible grasping;
ninth is the contemplation of non-attachment to the inexhaustible;
tenth is the contemplation of correspondence with the inexhaustible.
Eleventh is the contemplation on the inexhaustible nature of wisdom at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Son of good family!
These are called the eleven kinds of inexhaustible contemplations of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The treatise states:
The Sūtra says, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have eleven kinds of inexhaustible contemplations.
What are these eleven?"
"Contemplation on the inexhaustibility of the single body" means contemplating, according to reality, the conditioned and unconditioned bodies of both the noble and the non-noble.
"Second, contemplation on the inexhaustibility of phenomena" means contemplating, according to reality, the meanings of the real and the unreal.
"Third, the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of afflictions" refers to contemplating pure and defiled phenomena as they truly are.
"Fourth, the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of phenomena" refers to contemplating all phenomena—superior, middling, and inferior—as they truly are.
"5. The contemplation on the inexhaustibility of craving" refers to contemplating wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as they truly are.
"6. The contemplation on the inexhaustibility of views" refers to contemplating perverted and non-perverted views as they truly are.

"Seventh, the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of the aids to the path" means that one contemplates with suchness as one gathers roots of goodness through various gateways and dedicates them toward great enlightenment.
"Eighth, the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of grasping" means that one contemplates with suchness the boundless realm of sentient beings.
"Regarding the ninth, 'the contemplation of non-attachment to the inexhaustible': the meaning of non-attachment is as previously explained.
